questions.question: What ordering guarantee should an application assume for a Kafka topic?
options: All records in the topic have one global order
Records are ordered within each partition
Records are ordered only within each consumer group
Records are ordered by wall-clock timestamp across brokers
questions.explanation: Each partition is one ordered append-only log. A multi-partition topic has no single global order, so the record key defines the entity-level ordering boundary.

questions.question: A topic receives 90,000 events/second across 24 partitions. What is the average rate per partition before accounting for skew?
options: 2,400 events/second
3,750 events/second
24,000 events/second
90,000 events/second
questions.explanation: Average rate is 90,000 divided by 24, which is 3,750 events/second. A production design must still measure the hottest partition because keys rarely distribute perfectly.

questions.question: A consumer group has 24 partitions and 30 healthy consumer instances. How many instances can actively own a partition at one time?
questions.explanation: Within one consumer group, a partition is assigned to at most one member at a time. Six instances are idle unless the partition count or subscription changes.

questions.question: Why pair acks=all with a meaningful min.insync.replicas value?
options: To force every consumer to commit synchronously
To reject writes when too few caught-up replicas can satisfy the durability contract
To create one global order across all topic partitions
To remove the need for topic replication
questions.explanation: The minimum ISR turns an unsafe degraded write into visible unavailability. The application can then retry or fail deliberately without accepting a record below its chosen replica threshold.

questions.question: The broker appended a batch but its response was lost. What does producer idempotence protect when the client retries through the producer protocol?
options: It prevents the broker retry from appending a second copy in the log
It deduplicates every future application request with the same payload
It makes an unrelated database update exactly once
It removes the need for acknowledgements
questions.explanation: Producer idempotence lets Kafka identify protocol retries from that producer session. It does not infer business identity for new application sends or control external side effects.

questions.question: A consumer updates a payment database and crashes before committing its offset. What is the safest recovery boundary?
options: Commit offsets before processing every record
Disable retries so the record is never seen again
Use a stable operation ID and commit deduplication plus the payment mutation atomically
Increase topic retention until duplicate payments disappear
questions.explanation: The record will be replayed because Kafka does not know the database write succeeded. An idempotency record and business mutation in one destination transaction make that replay safe.

questions.question: Which cleanup policy best preserves the latest known value for every key over a long period?
options: Delete retention only
Log compaction
Shorter segment rolls only
Consumer offset commits
questions.explanation: Log compaction retains the latest value per key over time. It runs asynchronously, so consumers must still tolerate multiple historical versions during the compaction window.

questions.question: Which signal most directly says a consumer is failing the end-user freshness contract?
options: The topic has more than one partition
End-to-end event age is growing beyond its objective
The producer uses compression
The broker page cache is warm
questions.explanation: Offset lag is useful, but event age connects backlog to user-visible staleness. Growing age means the business effect is arriving later even when the raw offset count is hard to interpret.
